briefs.vegan:
Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies

name the vitamin by its sign · fat-soluble: why fat is not absorbed · water-soluble: what the patient drinks, takes or does not eat · the vegan diet: what must be supplementedWhich organ pattern names the vitamin, and why is this patient short of it?

RecognizeWorkupManagementPractice
Bottom line

Name the vitamin by its sign, then ask why this patient is short of it.

  • Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K): absorbed only with bile and pancreatic enzymes, so any fat malabsorption can deplete all four: cystic fibrosis (CF) and other pancreatic insufficiency, cholestasis and biliary atresia, celiac disease and inflammatory bowel disease, gastric bypass or short bowel.
  • Water-soluble (B and C): the body stores little, except B12 (cobalamin), so deficiency follows chronic alcohol use, poor intake, malabsorption (bypass, short bowel, Crohn disease) or a drug.
  • Vitamin K deficiency: the PT (prothrombin time) lengthens first, because factor VII (proconvertin) has the shortest half-life; the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) follows only when deficiency is severe, and platelets stay normal.
  • B12 or folate: both cause a megaloblastic anemia; neurologic signs and a high methylmalonic acid mark B12.
  • Unfortified vegan diet: B12 always, plus vitamin D and calcium, must be supplemented; iron and zinc join the list for children and menstruating women.
  • Order of treatment: thiamine before or with glucose; no folate alone until the B12 level is known, since folate corrects the anemia but not the nerve damage.
Recognize: name it by its sign
Each vitamin: who gets it and the sign that names it
VitaminWho gets itThe sign

Dry beriberi: symmetric sensorimotor neuropathy. Wet beriberi: high-output heart failure with edema
B3 (niacin)Alcohol use, anorexia, Crohn disease, Hartnup disease, carcinoid syndrome (tryptophan diverted to serotonin)Pellagra: photosensitive dermatitis of the neck (Casal necklace), hands and face, with diarrhea and dementia
B6 (pyridoxine)Isoniazid, alcohol usePeripheral neuropathy, cheilitis, stomatitis; seizures when severe; microcytic (sideroblastic) anemia
B9 (folate)Alcohol use, pregnancy, hemolysis, poor intake; methotrexate, trimethoprim, triamterene, phenytoin, valproate, carbamazepineMegaloblastic anemia with a normal neurologic exam; neural tube defects in pregnancy

CNo fruits or vegetables: food-selective child (autism), alcohol use, severe malnutritionSwollen bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, poor wound healing, a limp in children from bleeding under the periosteum; platelets, PT and aPTT normal
Bleeding: which pathway Vitamin K deficiency – PT/INR (international normalized ratio) prolonged first, aPTT normal or prolonged if severe, platelets and factor V normal · Liver failure – PT prolonged with a low factor V (factor V does not need vitamin K) and low albumin; the PT does not correct with vitamin K · Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) – sepsis, trauma or malignancy; a critically ill patient oozing from lines; platelets and fibrinogen low, PT and aPTT prolonged, D-dimer high
Vegan diet (unfortified) Must supplement – B12 (no unfortified plant source), vitamin D (skin synthesis covers only about half the requirement, less in northern latitudes) and calcium (plant calcium, as in spinach, is oxalate-bound and poorly absorbed) · At risk – iron and zinc in children (growth) and menstruating women; non-heme iron absorbs poorly, so pair it with vitamin C · Not deficient – folate (greens, legumes, fruit) and protein with essential amino acids in balanced diets
Workup
Vitamin D Measure – 25-hydroxyvitamin D, made in the liver; skip 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, often normal in deficiency because parathyroid hormone (PTH) drives its production · Rickets labs – alkaline phosphatase and PTH rise, 25-hydroxyvitamin D falls; phosphate is low (less absorbed, more lost in urine); calcium is low or normal, because PTH defends it
Management
By vitamin Vitamin K – parenteral for severe coagulopathy; add fresh frozen plasma for serious bleeding (intracranial, gastrointestinal or at several sites); in CF, restart pancreatic enzymes and fat-soluble vitamins · Newborn – one intramuscular dose of vitamin K at birth · Vitamin D – 50,000 international units (IU) weekly for 8 weeks, then 800 to 1,000 IU daily; recheck 25-hydroxyvitamin D in 3 to 4 months, aiming for 20 ng/mL or more; 400 IU daily for every infant in the first year · Thiamine – IV, before or with any glucose, in Wernicke encephalopathy or any malnourished or alcohol-using patient · B12 – intramuscular or high-dose oral; with neurologic signs, never folate alone · Folate – oral folic acid once the B12 level is known, or with B12 when the cause is unclear; alongside methotrexate; 0.4 mg daily for anyone who could become pregnant, 4 mg after a prior neural tube defect, starting before conception · B6 and C – pyridoxine with isoniazid; oral vitamin C, improving within days to weeks
Practice
  1. 24-year-old woman asks which supplements she needs strict vegan diet of unprocessed, unfortified plant foods Takes no supplements; eats legumes, greens and grains daily No fatigue, numbness or bone pain BP 112/70 mm Hg · hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL → Vitamin B12 → no unfortified plant source of B12 exists, so it must always be supplemented. Legumes, greens and grains supply abundant folate and protein, and balanced vegan diets supply complete protein, so neither folic acid nor protein needs supplementing; folate matters in pregnancy, but vegan diets are folate-rich
  2. 3-day-old boy has oozing from the umbilical stump dark stools since this morning Born at home; exclusively breastfed; parents declined newborn injections Well-appearing · platelets and fibrinogen normal · PT markedly prolonged · aPTT mildly prolonged → Vitamin K deficiency bleeding → a well newborn with no prophylaxis, normal platelets and fibrinogen and a long PT has vitamin K deficiency bleeding: parenteral vitamin K, with fresh frozen plasma if bleeding is serious; breast milk is low in vitamin K. Disseminated intravascular coagulation consumes platelets and fibrinogen in a critically ill patient. Hemophilia A lacks factor VIII (antihemophilic factor), which does not need vitamin K; it prolongs the aPTT and leaves the PT normal
  3. 47-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has 2 months of watery diarrhea worsening forgetfulness sharply bordered, scaly, darkened rash on the backs of the hands, the face and a band around the neck All sun-exposed; no blisters Afebrile → Niacin deficiency → photosensitive dermatitis with diarrhea and dementia is pellagra, the 4 Ds ending in death, and alcohol use is a leading cause. Porphyria cutanea tarda is also photosensitive, but it blisters on the backs of the hands and brings no diarrhea or dementia. Thiamine deficiency strikes the brain, eyes, gait or heart, not the skin
  4. 18-month-old boy walked late, only last month Exclusively breastfed with no supplements; dark skin; rarely outdoors bowed legs and widened wrists beading along the costochondral junctions Afebrile · calcium low-normal · phosphate low · alkaline phosphatase high → Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D → nutritional rickets: 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the form measured, and it falls in deficiency; replace vitamin D. 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is often normal, because PTH drives its production, and PTH holds calcium low or normal, so neither confirms the cause
  5. 52-year-old man with heavy daily alcohol use is brought in confused and unsteady horizontal nystagmus and weak lateral gaze in both eyes wide-based gait Afebrile · BP 128/80 mm Hg · fingerstick glucose 58 mg/dL → Intravenous thiamine before or with dextrose → confusion, eye findings and ataxia in a drinker is Wernicke encephalopathy: IV thiamine goes in before or with the dextrose, because a glucose load can precipitate or worsen it. The glucose is needed, but not first; oral thiamine at discharge misses the emergency, which needs IV thiamine on suspicion
  6. 16-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has 3 days of nosebleeds bruises easily for 2 months Off her prescribed medications; low-grade fever last week no organomegaly; neurologic exam normal Normal vital signs · platelet count normal → Absent coagulation factor activation → in CF the prescribed medications are usually pancreatic enzymes and fat-soluble vitamins; off them, fat is not absorbed, and without vitamin K the liver cannot gamma-carboxylate (activate) factors II, VII, IX (Christmas factor) and X, so the PT lengthens first: give vitamin K. Consumption (disseminated intravascular coagulation) needs a critically ill patient with low platelets; the recent fever is the decoy. Vitamin C is water soluble, so pancreatic insufficiency does not deplete it, and scurvy leaves the PT normal
  7. 15-year-old girl who follows a vegan diet has 3 months of fatigue heavy menstrual periods pale conjunctivae Takes no supplements or medications Afebrile · hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 71 fL → Iron deficiency → menstruating vegans are an at-risk group for iron; non-heme plant iron absorbs poorly, so supplement it and pair it with vitamin C. Vitamin B12 deficiency is macrocytic, not microcytic. Vitamin B6 deficiency can cause a microcytic (sideroblastic) anemia, but it follows isoniazid or alcohol use, with neuropathy
  8. 14-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has 6 months of falls Skips her pancreatic enzymes wide-based gait, positive Romberg, lost vibration and position sense absent ankle reflexes Hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL · MCV 88 fL · reticulocytes high · echocardiogram normal → Vitamin E deficiency → fat malabsorption depletes vitamin E: dorsal column and cerebellar damage with hemolysis (normal MCV, high reticulocytes); replace vitamin E. Vitamin B12 deficiency is megaloblastic and adds spastic weakness. Vitamin E deficiency mimics Friedreich ataxia, but here the cause is in sight: cystic fibrosis off enzymes, with hemolysis, and the echocardiogram is normal
  9. 67-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes on metformin has 2 months of fatigue mild numbness of the feet Hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL · MCV 108 fL · hypersegmented neutrophils · serum B12 240 pg/mL · folate normal → Serum methylmalonic acid → a megaloblastic anemia with a B12 of 200 to 300 pg/mL needs methylmalonic acid, and a high level confirms B12 deficiency; metformin is a cause. Homocysteine is high in both B12 and folate deficiency, so it cannot separate them. Intrinsic factor antibodies look for the cause (pernicious anemia) once the deficiency is shown
  10. 23-year-old woman has daily headaches and blurred vision Took several high-dose vitamin A supplements for acne for 4 months bilateral papilledema Body mass index 22 kg/m2 · brain imaging normal · opening pressure high, fluid normal → Excess vitamin A intake → vitamin A toxicity from supplements or retinoids causes pseudotumor cerebri (headache, papilledema, high opening pressure): stop the supplements and check for pregnancy, since vitamin A is teratogenic. Excess vitamin D causes hypercalcemia, not raised pressure, and a normal body mass index argues against obesity-related intracranial hypertension
  11. 6-year-old boy with autism has refused to walk for 3 weeks, citing leg pain Eats only white bread, crackers and cheese swollen, bleeding gums; perifollicular hemorrhages; coiled hairs Hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL · white cells and platelets normal · PT and aPTT normal → Vitamin C deficiency → scurvy, from impaired collagen hydroxylation: a food-selective child with bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs and a limp from bleeding under the periosteum; give oral vitamin C. It mimics acute lymphoblastic leukemia, but normal white cells, platelets and coagulation studies with gum disease point to the diet. Vitamin K deficiency lengthens the PT; scurvy leaves it normal
  12. 26-year-old man who follows a vegan diet has diffuse bone aches proximal muscle weakness Lives in a northern state; takes no supplements Afebrile · calcium low-normal · phosphate low · alkaline phosphatase high → Vitamin D deficiency → skin synthesis covers only about half the vitamin D requirement, less in northern latitudes, and an unfortified vegan diet adds little: osteomalacia with bone pain and proximal weakness. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis and dorsal-column signs, not bone pain. Primary hyperparathyroidism raises calcium; here calcium is low-normal, held there by PTH
  13. 4-week-old boy has oozing from his circumcision site since yesterday large scalp bruise Born at home; exclusively breastfed; parents declined all newborn injections Well-appearing · platelets normal · PT markedly prolonged · aPTT prolonged → Parenteral vitamin K → vitamin K deficiency bleeding: give parenteral vitamin K, the route for a severe coagulopathy, adding fresh frozen plasma for serious bleeding; oral vitamin K with a recheck in a week is too slow. Factor VIII treats hemophilia A; it does not need vitamin K and is not the missing factor
  14. 61-year-old man with long-standing alcohol use disorder cannot form new memories Hospitalized 3 months ago for confusion, eye-movement weakness and ataxia invents detailed accounts of recent days Steady gait · HR 78/min · alert and attentive · eye movements normal · no asterixis → Korsakoff syndrome → anterograde amnesia with confabulation in an alert drinker marks progression to Korsakoff syndrome (mammillary bodies), often permanent. Wernicke encephalopathy needs confusion, ophthalmoplegia or ataxia, and these have cleared. Hepatic encephalopathy ranges from subtle cognitive change to confusion and coma, with asterixis typically in its intermediate stages; he has no asterixis and is alert and attentive
  15. 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has fatigue Takes weekly methotrexate; stopped her folic acid no numbness or gait change Hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL · MCV 112 fL · hypersegmented neutrophils · serum B12 450 pg/mL · neurologic exam normal → Resume folic acid → methotrexate is a folate antagonist (a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor), and folic acid is given alongside it: resume it. A B12 over 300 pg/mL is sufficient and the neurologic exam is normal, so intramuscular B12 replaces nothing missing. The cause is already in sight, so a bone marrow biopsy adds nothing
  16. 47-year-old woman has 5 months of unsteadiness, numb feet Gastric bypass 6 years ago; off supplements 2 years thin, lighter hair; broad-based gait; positive Romberg lost vibration and position sense; brisk knee reflexes Hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL · B12, methylmalonic acid normal → Copper deficiency → copper deficiency after bypass mimics B12 deficiency, with ataxia, weakness and neuropathy plus fragile, depigmented hair: check copper when B12 and methylmalonic acid are normal, replace it and resume supplements. Vitamin E deficiency brings hemolysis and a neuropathy with hyporeflexia, not brisk reflexes
  17. 2-year-old boy is raised on the family's unprocessed vegan diet Takes vitamin B12 and vitamin D drops growing along the 50th percentile Eats legumes, greens, grains and fruit Afebrile · hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL → Iron and zinc → rapid growth raises requirements, so iron and zinc join the list for children, as for menstruating women. Greens, legumes and fruit supply folate, and balanced vegan diets supply protein and essential amino acids
  18. 44-year-old woman on phenytoin for epilepsy: 4 months of aching hips, thighs Walks outdoors daily; drinks milk trouble climbing stairs; tender pelvis Calcium low-normal · phosphate low · alkaline phosphatase, PTH high · 25-hydroxyvitamin D 9 ng/mL · creatinine, albumin, liver enzymes normal → Accelerated hepatic breakdown of vitamin D → phenytoin, carbamazepine, isoniazid and rifampin speed the breakdown of vitamin D: drug-induced deficiency with osteomalacia despite sun and milk; replace vitamin D. A normal creatinine argues against chronic kidney disease (impaired renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation), and a normal albumin and liver enzymes against chronic liver disease (impaired hepatic 25-hydroxylation)
  19. 38-year-old woman has 3 weeks of burning and tingling in both feet Taking isoniazid alone for latent tuberculosis for 3 months; no other supplement decreased pinprick sensation in a stocking distribution Afebrile · liver enzymes normal → Add pyridoxine → isoniazid causes a B6 deficiency neuropathy, and pyridoxine is given with isoniazid: add it. Switching to rifampin is not needed, because the neuropathy comes from a missing vitamin that pyridoxine replaces, and gabapentin treats the symptom, not the deficiency
  20. 62-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has new oozing from IV sites Admitted with pneumonia; 10 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics and little oral intake INR 2.6 · aPTT mildly prolonged · platelets 140,000/mm3 → Factor V activity → both causes can lengthen his PT: antibiotics and poor intake cut vitamin K, and cirrhosis cuts synthesis. Factor V does not need vitamin K, so a normal factor V points to vitamin K deficiency and a low one to hepatic synthetic failure. Factor VII depends on vitamin K, so it falls in vitamin K deficiency and cannot clear the liver; a mixing study separates a factor deficiency from an inhibitor, which is not the question
  21. 30-year-old woman who follows a vegan diet has 4 months of numb feet Takes no supplements loss of vibratory sense in both feet Afebrile · hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL · MCV 109 fL → Vitamin B12 deficiency → B12 has no unfortified plant source; macrocytosis plus dorsal-column signs (subacute combined degeneration) is B12 deficiency, and its neurologic signs can appear before the anemia. Folate deficiency causes macrocytosis alone, with a normal neurologic exam, and iron deficiency is microcytic
  22. 1-hour-old boy born at term after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery Mother plans to breastfeed exclusively Parents ask about routine newborn care Well-appearing · Apgar scores 8 and 9 · HR 140/min · T 37.0 °C → Single intramuscular dose of vitamin K → one intramuscular dose of vitamin K at birth prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding, and breast milk is low in vitamin K; the single intramuscular dose, not an oral dose, is the prophylaxis, and waiting for bleeding gives up prevention
  23. 24-year-old woman at 11 weeks' gestation is confused and unsteady 4 weeks of vomiting, 6 kg lost; intravenous dextrose twice horizontal nystagmus, weak lateral gaze bilaterally BP 104/66 mm Hg · no headache or papilledema · sodium 134 mEq/L, stable → Wernicke encephalopathy → confusion, eye findings and ataxia after weeks of hyperemesis gravidarum and dextrose loads is Wernicke encephalopathy: IV thiamine before further dextrose. Osmotic demyelination follows rapid correction of hyponatremia, and this sodium has not moved. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis brings headache in 80 to 90%, and papilledema may join it when pressure rises significantly; she has neither
  24. 9-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis cannot see well at dusk Skips his pancreatic enzymes and vitamin supplements dry conjunctivae and cornea; Bitot spots on both eyes dry skin Afebrile · gait and reflexes normal → Vitamin A deficiency → cystic fibrosis off enzymes means fat malabsorption, which depletes vitamin A: night blindness, dry conjunctivae and cornea (xerophthalmia), Bitot spots and dry skin; one fat-soluble deficiency means all four need checking or replacing. Vitamin E deficiency brings ataxia and lost vibration sense with hemolysis, and his gait and reflexes are normal. Retinitis pigmentosa also brings night blindness, but the front-of-eye signs here (dry conjunctivae and cornea, Bitot spots) are the vitamin A signs, and the cause is in sight
  25. 22-month-old girl walked late and now waddles Still drinks mostly breast milk; never had vitamin D drops bowed legs; thickened wrists and ankles Afebrile · HR 110/min · weight at the 40th percentile → Phosphorus concentration → vitamin D deficiency rickets: phosphate falls, because less is absorbed and PTH increases its loss in the urine. PTH and alkaline phosphatase both rise; osteoblasts release the enzyme as they lay down bone matrix
  26. 27-year-old woman is planning a pregnancy Her first pregnancy was affected by anencephaly Healthy; takes no medications; eats a varied diet BP 114/72 mm Hg · body mass index 23 kg/m2 → Folic acid 4 mg daily starting before conception → after a prior neural tube defect pregnancy the dose is 4 mg daily, started before conception; 0.4 mg daily is for anyone who could become pregnant, and the first prenatal visit is too late to start
  27. 74-year-old woman in a nursing home has 3 months of aching hips and thighs Rarely goes outside trouble rising from a chair; tender bones Afebrile · 25-hydroxyvitamin D 8 ng/mL · calcium normal · kidney function normal → Vitamin D 50,000 IU weekly for 8 weeks → osteomalacia from vitamin D deficiency: 50,000 IU weekly for 8 weeks, then 800 to 1,000 IU daily, rechecking the level in 3 to 4 months. A daily 1,000 IU is the maintenance dose, not the load. Calcitriol, a vitamin D analog, treats low calcium and bone disease when the kidneys or parathyroid glands are not working; her kidney function and calcium are normal
How NBME framed it: question 1

5-day-old boy with bleeding from vitamin K deficiency bleeding from the nose, mouth and gastrointestinal tract subdural hemorrhage Vitamin K therapy is being given

In addition to vitamin K, which is the next step?

Competing answers
  • Cryoprecipitate: a blood product for bleeding; but it carries fibrinogen, factors VIII and XIII (fibrin-stabilizing factor) and von Willebrand factor, not II, VII, IX or X.
  • Lactated Ringer solution: he is losing blood from several sites; but it restores volume and carries no clotting factors.
  • Platelets: a bleeding newborn; but vitamin K deficiency leaves the platelet count normal, so they replace nothing missing.

Down to two: fresh frozen plasma or factor VIII concentrate. Fresh frozen plasma replaces factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S at once, while vitamin K restores them over hours. Factor VIII concentrate treats hemophilia A, and factor VIII does not need vitamin K. The lead-in grants vitamin K, so only the blood product is tested; factor VIII concentrate is the bait.

How NBME framed it: question 2

15-month-old girl has not begun to crawl or walk Exclusively breastfed since birth Length at the 50th and weight at the 85th percentile; language and social skills normal for age widened wrists; examination otherwise normal

Which serum finding is most likely to be increased?

Competing answers
  • Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) activity: a liver enzyme beside alkaline phosphatase; but it rises with liver cell injury; a high alkaline phosphatase with normal ALT and GGT (gamma-glutamyl transferase) comes from bone.
  • Calcium concentration: a bone mineral; but PTH holds it low or normal; a high calcium points to hyperparathyroidism or vitamin D excess.
  • Magnesium concentration: a mineral tied to calcium balance; but vitamin D deficiency does not raise it; a low magnesium impairs PTH secretion and action.

Down to two: alkaline phosphatase activity or phosphorus concentration. Alkaline phosphatase: osteoblasts make it as they lay down matrix, and it is high in active rickets, often before calcium or phosphate falls. Phosphorus falls instead, because absorption drops and PTH increases urinary loss; a high phosphate points to kidney failure or hypoparathyroidism. The key was an enzyme activity set among minerals and a liver enzyme, and the infant's rickets showed only as late crawling and walking with widened wrists.

Brain and skin Wernicke triad – confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia; often incomplete, so one or two features in a drinker is enough to treat · Korsakoff – anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation and no insight, older long-term memories relatively preserved; it marks progression (mammillary bodies) and is often permanent · Pellagra, the 4 Ds – dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, death · Thiamine level – skip it before treating suspected Wernicke: the result is not back in time, so give IV (intravenous) thiamine on suspicion
Toxicity: only A and D Vitamin A – from excess liver, supplements or retinoids: pseudotumor cerebri (headache, papilledema, high opening pressure), bone pain and fractures, hepatomegaly, dry skin and alopecia, and teratogenicity, the reason isotretinoin needs pregnancy testing and contraception · Vitamin D – hypercalcemia, from massive overdose or from granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis, where macrophages make 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D without PTH control; 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is the level to order for hypercalcemia with suspected sarcoidosis or lymphoma
Vitamin D deficiency: causes Poor intake (milk avoidance, lactose intolerance, unfortified vegan diet); malabsorption (Crohn disease, celiac disease, gastrectomy or bariatric surgery); little sun (high latitude, dark skin, indoor life, nursing home, night work); obesity and older age; chronic kidney and liver disease; phenytoin, carbamazepine, isoniazid and rifampin, which speed its breakdown.
Common wrong answers Increased platelet sequestration: CF liver disease can enlarge the spleen, but sequestration lowers platelets without lengthening the PT. Reduced von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease activity: TTP is acute, with thrombocytopenia, hemolysis and neurologic signs. Homocysteine to separate B12 from folate: high in both; only methylmalonic acid separates them. Folic acid for a megaloblastic anemia with numb feet: the blood improves, but the neurologic signs mark B12, and folate alone lets them progress. Vitamin K for bleeding gums: scurvy leaves the PT normal. Folic acid for a vegan: it matters in pregnancy, but vegan diets are folate-rich. Dextrose first in a confused drinker: needed, but thiamine goes in before or with it.
After gastric bypass Supplements and periodic levels are lifelong, because deficiencies overlap: B12 (macrocytic anemia, neuropathy, cognitive change); A (night blindness), D and calcium (bone loss with secondary hyperparathyroidism), K (coagulopathy); iron (anemia; the duodenum is bypassed); zinc (alopecia, rash, night blindness); copper (ataxia, weakness and neuropathy that mimic B12 deficiency, with fragile, depigmented hair; check copper when B12 and methylmalonic acid are normal); folate (macrocytic anemia); thiamine (Wernicke, especially with intractable vomiting).
Pearls One malabsorption cause usually depletes several fat-soluble vitamins, so a CF or cholestatic patient with one deficiency needs all four checked or replaced. Vitamin A supplementation is standard in severe measles and where deficiency is endemic. Broad-spectrum antibiotics cut gut bacterial production of vitamin K. Factor VII has the shortest half-life (about 6 hours), then IX (Christmas factor), X and II (about 60 hours); protein C is also short (about 8 hours), so starting warfarin lowers it first and briefly makes blood hypercoagulable, the reason for heparin bridging and the cause of warfarin skin necrosis. Without vitamin K, the liver cannot gamma-carboxylate factors II, VII, IX and X. Fresh frozen plasma replaces them and proteins C and S at once; vitamin K restores them over hours. B12 neurologic signs can appear before the anemia. Rarer B vitamins: B2 (riboflavin) causes angular cheilitis, stomatitis, glossitis and a normocytic anemia; B5 (pantothenic acid), rare, distal paresthesias; B7 (biotin), rare, from raw egg whites, alopecia and dermatitis. The vegan diet also lowers glucose and cholesterol and reduces cardiovascular risk; on the exam, a well-planned vegan diet is credited as nutritionally adequate except for B12.
Vitamin D thresholds: current status Checked September 2026. In force: the Institute of Medicine 2011 cutoffs, still used by the National Institutes of Health Office of Dietary Supplements and matched by the 2016 Global Consensus on nutritional rickets: under 12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L) deficient, 12 to under 20 inadequate, 20 or more adequate, over 50 ng/mL a risk of harm. Retired: the Endocrine Society 2011 set (under 20 deficient, 21 to 29 insufficient, 30 to 100 sufficient); its 2024 guideline endorses no cutoff or target of 30 and advises against routine testing in healthy people. In 2024 it advised empiric supplementation above the daily allowance at ages 1 to 18, over 75, in pregnancy and in high-risk prediabetes; adults 19 to 74 take the usual allowance (600 IU, 800 IU over 70). Unchanged: treat symptomatic deficiency (rickets, osteomalacia) whatever the cutoff. On the exam, older questions may use the 20 and 30 cutoffs, so read the level against the symptoms. Most deficiency is silent or causes vague aches and surfaces as low bone density, fracture or osteomalacia. The vitamin D pathway: skin makes it from 7-dehydrocholesterol with ultraviolet light and diet adds more; the kidney 1-alpha-hydroxylase, driven by PTH and suppressed by high calcium, makes the active form, which raises intestinal calcium absorption (its main action) and renal calcium and phosphate reabsorption, mineralizes bone and suppresses PTH.
Pairs with Part I Recurrent Respiratory Infection and Structural Lung Disease: is growth poor with greasy stools, and is the sweat chloride high? Part I Hemophilia: is the PT or the aPTT long, and are platelets normal? Part I Night Blindness: vitamin A against retinitis pigmentosa; is the front of the eye normal? Part I Hypercalcemia: vitamin D excess and sarcoidosis; is the 25-hydroxy or the 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D high? Feeding an Infant or Toddler: vitamin D 400 IU for breastfed infants. Part II Fever and Rash in a Child: measles. Part I Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment: the papilledema workup and the other drugs that raise intracranial pressure; is the papilledema bilateral with full visual fields? Part I Tall Stature and Marfanoid Habitus: inherited high homocysteine, treated with B6, folate and B12. Part I Teratogenic Exposures: folate-antagonist antiepileptics and neural tube defects. Part I Tuberculosis: isoniazid with B6.
Transferable rule

Read the organ pattern first: eye, bone, dorsal columns with hemolysis, bleeding, brain and eyes, sun-exposed skin with diarrhea, megaloblastic blood, or bleeding gums with normal clotting. Then ask what the patient drinks, takes or does not eat, or why fat is not absorbed. For a diet, ask where each nutrient physically comes from: no unfortified plant source means it must be supplemented. Give thiamine before glucose, and settle B12 before folate alone.
